searchText: seems like kate commitments will work here as long as you have a deterministic mapping from the natural numbers to your elements A B C D you can use them for a vector commitment so if you vector is [ A B C X ] then you can prove any subset in a single proof and can prove exclusion for D by showing it evaluates to X Yes, the elements have a deterministic ordering, so I think we can use the vector commitment. Say the committer (Alice) generates a commitment for [A, B, C, Q] Can Bob generate a proof for C without knowing Q (or B without C & Q)? yup, thats the direct case of kzg, just proving that the polynomial committed to evaluates to that element at that point, `f(x) = y` you can batch proofs but you need more polynomial manipulations on top of the "basic" proof so you'd have a commitment C to the polynomial formed by Lagrange interpolation of your data `{0:A, 1:B, 2:C, 3:Q}` then the "opening" is a proof (along w/ the value if needed) that the polynomial indeed evaluates to say `C` at the point `2` It seems like Bob would need to know Q to generate the lagrange interpolation, no? Alice needs it ah i misread, Bob is not the verifier so Alice could make the commitment w/ all of the set of elements Alice could make a proof about one element w/o having to say anything about the others i'm not really sure who is Bob is separately from Alice you do need the full polynomial (all of the elements) to make a proof
